how: Computers played each other with the real rules (Clue rules, 4 players unless noted). The tested computer took every seat in turn so going first didn't skew it. Measured 2026-10-27 with tools/sim.js after Hard got stronger. A fair share is 25% with 4 players.

vs.label: Hard vs 3 Medium
vs.note: 2000 games. Fair share is 25%. Was 33% before Hard learned to accuse a little sooner and to read the other computers' questions. About 68% one-on-one.

vs.label: Hard vs 2 Medium
vs.note: 2000 games, 3 players. Fair share is 33%. Was 43%.

vs.label: Hard vs 5 Medium
vs.note: 1000 games, 6 players. Fair share is 17%. Was 21%.

vs.label: Hard vs Medium, 2 players
vs.note: 1000 games, the 2-player rules (four cards face down in rooms). Fair share is 50%. Hard drags its rival's pawn away with its questions; without that it was 50%.

house.how: 600 games each, 2026-10-28, tools/sim.js with the house rule named. The ladder Hard > Medium > Easy holds under every option.
rows: Medium vs 3 Easy 77.2%, Hard vs 3 Easy 85.3%

seatHow: 400 games, four Medium computers, Clue rules. Each bar is how often that seat won.
seatNote: Going first is worth about 7 points over a fair 25%: the first player gets the first question in.
length: With 4 players a game takes about 35 turns, so about 9 turns each. With the newer rules (2 dice, move up to the roll) it drops to about 20 turns.
